hints: Notice the solvent controls what the hydroxide ion does, acting as a base in one case and as a nucleophile in the other.
Ethanolic NaOH favours elimination of HBr to form an alkene, while aqueous NaOH favours substitution of Br by OH to form an alcohol.
Ask yourself if a diol with two OH groups could ever form from one Br atom in one step with NaOH.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two roles of NaOH**

Hydroxide can act as a base (removes H+) causing elimination, or as a nucleophile (donates to carbon) causing substitution. The solvent decides which wins.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{ethanolic NaOH} \rightarrow \text{elimination to alkene}$$
$$\text{aqueous NaOH} \rightarrow \text{substitution to alcohol}$$

**Check statement 1 - ethanolic to propene**

In ethanol, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base. It removes H from C-2 while Br leaves from C-1 in 1-bromopropane.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH (in ethanol)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
So statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 - aqueous to propan-1-ol**

In water, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a nucleophile and replaces Br by $S_N$ reaction. This is hydrolysis.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH (aq)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}$$
So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 - ethanolic to diol**

A diol like propane-1,2-diol has two OH groups. Starting from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ we have only one Br to replace, and elimination conditions do not add OH groups. Diols need cold alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ on an alkene, not NaOH on a haloalkane.

So statement 3 is incorrect, and the correct combination is 1 and 2 only.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statement 3. A diol cannot form from 1-bromopropane with ethanolic NaOH, there is only one Br to substitute and elimination conditions give propene, not addition of two OH groups.
options.B: Correct because statements 1 and 2 only are true. Ethanolic NaOH gives elimination to propene, and aqueous NaOH gives nucleophilic substitution to propan-1-ol. Statement 3 is false.
options.C: Incorrect because it includes statement 3 and misses statement 1. Statement 1 is definitely true (elimination in ethanol) and statement 3 is definitely false (no diol formation).
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only statement 1. Statement 2 is also true, aqueous NaOH hydrolyses 1-bromopropane to propan-1-ol by nucleophilic substitution.
